headline: Parliament Advances Restricted-Day Alcohol Bill as Cost-of-Living and Fiscal Disputes Intensify
summary: Parliament debated pressure on household budgets and public services, with opposition MPs challenging the Government over transport costs, unemployment, housing and access to counselling. Ministers defended their policies while the House also examined long-term fiscal risks, disputed the handling of COVID-era decisions and advanced changes to alcohol trading rules on restricted days. Two community trust bills also progressed, and Labour MP Peeni Henare delivered his valedictory address.

topicSummaries.topic: Cost-of-Living Claims Clash Over Transport, Fees and Council Rates
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The dispute concerns the daily costs people face for transport, vehicle ownership and local services, as well as who should be held responsible for rising bills.
topicSummaries.content: Opposition Leader Chris Hipkins challenged Prime Minister Christopher Luxon over increases to parking fines, vehicle levies, registration costs and fuel tax, as well as public transport funding cuts and reduced central-government support for councils. Luxon argued that excessive government spending had driven inflation and interest rates, and urged support for a rates cap and local-government reforms. He rejected Hipkins’ suggestion that withdrawn council funding had contributed to rates increases, while also pointing to projects the Government had stopped as examples of wasteful spending.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How did cutting public transport funding, forcing some commuters to pay up to 50 percent more to get to work or school, reduce the cost of living pressures on New Zealand families?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The major driver of the costs of living challenges that New Zealanders have been experiencing is actually the Government spending out of control, driving up inflation, driving up interest rates, putting the economy into a difficult place, and people losing their jobs.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Introduces Hours-Based Employment Leave Bill
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes would affect how workers accrue and use annual and sick leave, while aiming to reduce payroll errors and compliance costs for employers.
topicSummaries.content: Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden said the Employment Leave Bill had been introduced to replace the complex Holidays Act 2003. It would move annual and sick leave from a weeks-based entitlement system to accrual in hours, which the Government says would better suit people with variable work schedules. Van Velden said most people’s entitlements would remain similar, but the calculation method would change, and eligible workers would no longer have to wait six months for sick leave or 12 months for annual leave. The bill has entered Parliament for consideration.

keyExchanges.speaker: Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: The biggest change in the Employment Leave Bill is a switch from a weeks-based entitlement system to an hours-based accrual system for both annual leave and sick leave.

keyExchanges.speaker: Laura McClure (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: How is the Employment Leave Bill different from the current Holidays Act?

topicSummaries.topic: Housing Affordability Claims Meet Opposition Challenge on Homelessness
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Housing costs and access to secure accommodation affect household budgets and whether people can afford to rent or buy a home.
topicSummaries.content: Acting Housing Minister Tama Potaka cited Cotality and government indicators showing improved housing affordability, including a lower house-price-to-income ratio and reduced mortgage payments as a share of household income. He also said several measures showed rents were flat or falling, while opposition MPs raised concerns about homelessness and housing pressures. In response, Potaka pointed to Housing First support and said nearly 500 people had moved from rough sleeping into housing over the previous four months.

keyExchanges.speaker: Kieran McAnulty (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Can he confirm that front-line providers such as the Auckland City Mission, the Wellington City Mission, and the Christchurch Methodist Mission have told him to his face that homelessness has reached unprecedented heights and they point to his policies as to the reason why?

keyExchanges.speaker: Tama Potaka (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I can confirm that many community housing providers—including some in Auckland, Hamilton, Wellington, and Christchurch—have been very enthusiastic about the additional support that we have given for Housing First that has seen nearly 500 people come off the streets, out of rough sleeping, into housing over the last four months.

topicSummaries.topic: Jobseeker Numbers and Unemployment Remain a Point of Political Dispute
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The number of people seeking work affects household income and the demand for welfare and employment support.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Willie Jackson asked whether jobseeker numbers were higher or lower than when Social Development and Employment Minister Louise Upston took office, but Upston did not give a direct comparison. She said close to 190,000 people were on the benefit when the Government took office, that numbers had been rising since 2022, and that 83,000 people had left benefits for jobs. Upston said employment indicators showed signs of recovery and blamed earlier economic conditions; Jackson cited rising jobseeker numbers and high unemployment as evidence the Government’s approach was not working.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willie Jackson (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why should hard-working New Zealanders trust the Minister to fix unemployment and reduce job seekers when, under her watch, job seekers have increased every quarter, unemployment is at a 10-year high, and homelessness is out of control?

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This is a Government that has been absolutely focused on reducing excessive Government spending which led to higher levels of inflation, higher interest rates, which leads to unemployment.

topicSummaries.topic: Mental Health Debate Pits Access Statistics Against Counselling Costs
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Waiting times and the cost of counselling can determine whether people receive mental health support when they need it.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Ingrid Leary asked whether counselling costs and waits of up to six months were preventing people from accessing care. Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey responded with figures on access to primary and specialist services, workforce growth and the number of adults seen. He said primary counselling support had expanded from 200,000 to 250,000 people a year and that an accreditation pathway had enabled 330 more counsellors to work in publicly funded roles. Leary continued to question whether funding gaps were leaving people on waiting lists, while Doocey disputed her description of private counselling access.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ingrid Leary (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is he concerned that counsellors report that they could see more clients yet people remain stuck on waiting lists because funding is not available to them?

keyExchanges.speaker: Matt Doocey (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I’m happy to announce to the House that when you look at primary counselling support, when we came into office, that was sitting at 200,000 Kiwis a year; we’ve now grown that to 250,000 Kiwis a year.

topicSummaries.topic: Fire and Emergency Cost Efficiencies Draw Safety and Union Questions
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to firefighter staffing, training, equipment and pay could affect emergency response capacity and the safety of crews and the public.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Lemauga Lydia Sosene questioned whether proposed savings and restructuring at Fire and Emergency New Zealand could affect safety, citing reports of cancelled recruit courses, possible staffing reductions and equipment concerns. Internal Affairs Minister Brooke van Velden rejected the description of the changes as $50 million in annual cuts, saying the organisation was seeking efficiencies and had no final restructure decisions. She said front-line firefighters and communications-centre roles were not proposed to be affected and that $84.7 million was planned for trucks, property and equipment. Van Velden also linked partial pay deductions to escalating industrial action by the firefighters’ union and urged negotiators to return to talks.

keyExchanges.speaker: Lemauga Lydia Sosene (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Will cutting fire prevention staff, specialist wildfire roles, and key support staff for firefighters keep the public and firefighters safe?

keyExchanges.speaker: Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: Those are simply proposals, and there are no final decisions that have been made.

topicSummaries.topic: Ministers Step Up Fuel-Price Monitoring Amid Global Volatility
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Fuel prices feed directly into transport and business costs, making market oversight relevant to household budgets.
topicSummaries.content: Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Scott Simpson said he had asked the Commerce Commission to monitor wholesale and retail fuel prices and importer margins more frequently. Simpson and the Energy Minister had also written to fuel companies to emphasise fair pricing and clear communication. Simpson said the steps were intended to ensure price changes reflected genuine international market pressures rather than unjustified increases, and stressed that the letters were not accusations of misconduct.

keyExchanges.speaker: Scott Simpson (National)
keyExchanges.quote: In my letter, I asked the Commerce Commission to increase the frequency of its fuel price monitoring to closely watch pricing behaviour and margins and to engage with industry and consumers if any questionable behaviour emerges.

keyExchanges.speaker: Katie Nimon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: How do these steps help protect households and businesses while still supporting a competitive fuel market?

topicSummaries.topic: LNG Import Terminal Costs and Dry-Year Power Security Debated
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposal could affect electricity bills and the balance between reliable power supply and investment in renewable energy.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Scott Willis questioned whether volatile international liquefied natural gas prices could erase forecast savings from a proposed import terminal and why electricity users would help fund it. Energy Minister Simon Watts defended the terminal as insurance against dry-year electricity shortages, saying forward electricity prices had fallen since the announcement and that backup generation could reduce a risk premium in power bills. Willis argued that the cost savings were uncertain while household levies would be imposed, highlighting a dispute over who benefits and who pays.

keyExchanges.speaker: Scott Willis (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he accept that any cost savings from an LNG terminal are estimates only, and that the only thing guaranteed about an LNG terminal is that there will be extra costs levied on electricity users in New Zealand households?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simon Watts (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Again, that is a reflection that the market has confidence that the solution which this Government is going to undertake deals with the challenge and the problem which we have, which is lack of cover in a dry year.

topicSummaries.topic: Long-Term Fiscal Debate Highlights Ageing, Debt and Competing Policy Choices
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Decisions about debt, tax and spending will shape future funding for healthcare, retirement incomes, infrastructure and responses to economic or natural shocks.
topicSummaries.content: A special debate on Treasury’s long-term fiscal and investment statements focused on an ageing population, rising superannuation and healthcare costs, climate-related risks and the need to prepare for future shocks. Finance Minister Nicola Willis argued that returning to surplus and reducing debt would create room to respond to crises; Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour called for a smaller, more efficient Government and said difficult choices lay ahead. Labour MPs defended pandemic-era spending and promoted long-term public investment, while Green MPs argued for stronger climate action and more progressive revenue options. The debate ended with the House agreeing to take note of the committee report, rather than making a new policy decision.

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: An important first step is to create fiscal space for future shocks and choices by returning to surplus and bringing debt down to more prudent levels.

keyExchanges.speaker: Deborah Russell (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Twenty thousand New Zealanders are still alive—the lowest excess mortality rate in the world—businesses have survived; livelihoods that were protected. That’s what we have to show for it.

topicSummaries.topic: COVID Vaccine Advice and Mandates Fuel Accountability Dispute
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The exchange concerns what advice was available to decision-makers about vaccine requirements for teenagers and how government decisions are reviewed and explained.
topicSummaries.content: New Zealand First leader Winston Peters questioned Health Minister Simeon Brown about a royal commission finding that advice raising concerns from the COVID-19 Vaccine Technical Advisory Group was provided to Chris Hipkins in December 2021 and considered by Ayesha Verrall in January 2022. Brown said the report did not identify actions by former ministers following the advice and that he was not aware of any. He also confirmed that workplace vaccine mandates for the age group remained until late January 2022 and vaccine-certificate requirements until April. The Speaker ruled that some questions about former ministers’ conduct were not in order, while Brown said the Government would consider the inquiry’s recommendations and respond in July.

keyExchanges.speaker: Winston Peters (NZ First)
keyExchanges.quote: Did the royal commission find that the briefing received by Ministers on 22 December 2021, which raised concerns from the COVID-19 Vaccine Technical Advisory Group, was considered by the Hon Ayesha Verrall?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The royal commission found the briefing received by Ministers on 22 December 2021, which raised concerns from the COVID-19 Vaccine Technical Advisory Group, was considered by the Hon Ayesha Verrall on 7 January 2022.

topicSummaries.topic: Alcohol Bill Advances With On-Licence Amendment; Other Changes Rejected
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed rules would change when some bars, restaurants and RSAs can serve alcohol on restricted days, affecting hospitality businesses, patrons and local communities.
topicSummaries.content: The committee stage of Kieran McAnulty’s bill proposed allowing hospitality venues already permitted to open on Good Friday, Easter Sunday and Christmas Day to serve alcohol under their usual licensing conditions, and making it easier for RSAs to serve members of the public after Anzac services. Supporters said the current rules around substantial meals create confusion for staff and customers; opponents cited religious observance, family time and alcohol-harm concerns. The committee rejected amendments that would have widened the changes to more off-licence sales or removed the Easter and Christmas provisions. It approved an ACT amendment to address an interaction with shop-trading law, then reported the bill back to the House with amendments. The bill was not given its final reading that evening.

keyExchanges.speaker: Kieran McAnulty (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: It simply allows those that make a choice for them and their families, frankly, to be able to go to an on-licence.

keyExchanges.speaker: Jamie Arbuckle (NZ First)
keyExchanges.quote: What is wrong with asking for our families to actually be at home with family members, to enjoy Christmas, to enjoy Easter?

topicSummaries.topic: Eastern Bay Trust Bill Seeks Wider Grants for Community Causes
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: If approved, the change could make an estimated $1 million to $2 million more available each year for community organisations in the Eastern Bay of Plenty.
topicSummaries.content: National MP Dana Kirkpatrick’s private bill to broaden Trust Horizon’s grant-making powers passed its first reading and was referred to the Social Services and Community Committee. The trust is currently limited largely to energy-related purposes; the bill would allow support for a wider range of charitable activities and let future deed changes be considered by the High Court. Kirkpatrick said the trust expected the change to unlock additional annual community funding, and reported that 80.7 percent of respondents to a community poll supported it. Labour, the Greens and New Zealand First expressed support while raising issues for the select committee to examine, including maintaining energy projects and protecting the trust’s assets.

keyExchanges.speaker: Dana Kirkpatrick (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This private bill seeks to amend the terms of the trust deed to allow it to support a broader range of charitable activities within its district.

keyExchanges.speaker: Jo Luxton (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: We are supportive of this piece of legislation. We do see the benefits that it will bring to the community, and so we support it at this point, particularly to the select committee process.

topicSummaries.topic: Carter Trust Amendment Bill Passes Second Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The change is intended to keep a long-running Carterton charitable legacy operating under modern arrangements for aged care and community support.
topicSummaries.content: The House agreed to the second reading of the private Carter Trust Amendment Bill, which would wind up the historic trust and transfer its assets to the Carter Society and the Anglican Parish of Carterton. National MP Mike Butterick said the changes would help the society continue its aged-care work, while committee members said they had clarified provisions on fees and upkeep of Charles Rooking Carter’s grave. MPs from Labour, the Greens, ACT and New Zealand First supported the bill, and several noted that Parliament could consider a more streamlined process for similar trust updates.

keyExchanges.speaker: Mike Butterick (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The Carter Trust Amendment Bill is a private bill aimed at winding up the Carter Trust, amending its governing will, and enabling the distribution of its assets to the Carter Society and the Anglican Parish of Carterton.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ingrid Leary (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: All of those things can be true at the same time, and I just think it’s really important that when we look at a trust like this, we take into account all of the histories and all of the perspectives that attach to it.

topicSummaries.topic: Peeni Henare Delivers Valedictory After 12 Years in Parliament
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Henare’s departure marked the end of a parliamentary career spanning roles in health, civil defence, housing, Whānau Ora and defence.
topicSummaries.content: Labour MP Peeni Henare used his valedictory statement to thank constituents, colleagues, staff and whānau after 12 years in Parliament. He reflected on his work in Māori health, Whānau Ora, housing and emergency response, including the Whakaari / White Island eruption, and said Parliament should rebuild public trust and make space for more constructive cross-party engagement. The House then adjourned for a dinner break before resuming its legislative business.

keyExchanges.speaker: Peeni Henare (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: We must move beyond “gotcha”-style politics and actually engage across parties with mana and integrity.

conclusion: The House advanced several bills, but the day’s central tensions remained unresolved: how to ease immediate cost pressures while managing long-term fiscal risks, and how far to relax alcohol rules on traditionally restricted days.
